ministry: Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction / Technology and Innovation

audience.name: ADSP Platform Team
audience.description: The Government of Alberta ADSP technology team responsible for operating, monitoring, and enforcing compliance of the planner-service within the ADSP platform. They have deep ADSP platform architecture knowledge and high technical proficiency. They verify service compliance with mandatory platform patterns, monitor health and observability endpoints, enforce multi-tenant data isolation, and conduct security reviews.
goals: Verify planner-service compliance with ADSP platform patterns including initializePlatform(), Keycloak JWT, MongoDB, and RabbitMQ
Monitor service health and LLM API performance through structured observability endpoints
Enforce and audit multi-tenant data isolation at API and database layers
Review security audit logs and assess OWASP ASVS Level 2 conformance
Configure RBAC role policies and session inactivity timeout settings
outcomes: planner-service operates within the standard ADSP platform operational model without special-casing
All tenant data isolation requirements are provably enforced and auditable
Security events and administrative actions are tamper-evidently logged for compliance and incident response

journeys.name: Platform Compliance Verification for Production Onboarding
journeys.description: The ADSP Platform Team verifies that the planner-service satisfies all mandatory platform patterns before approving production deployment. This involves checking initializePlatform() SDK initialization, Keycloak JWT configuration, RabbitMQ domain event registration, MongoDB connectivity, multi-tenant data isolation enforcement, and RBAC role configuration.
journeys.trigger: A new planner-service build is submitted for platform onboarding review prior to production deployment
journeys.goal: Confirm planner-service satisfies every mandatory ADSP platform pattern and approve production promotion

steps.action: Review the planner-service startup logs to confirm initializePlatform() completes successfully and all required ADSP service registrations are present
needs: Access to planner-service structured JSON startup logs
ADSP platform compliance checklist specifying required initializePlatform() registrations
steps.touchpoint: planner-service Health Check Endpoints (/health/live, /health/ready) and structured JSON logging output
frontstage: Live and ready endpoint responses confirming service startup state
Structured JSON log entries showing initializePlatform() completion and ADSP SDK registration events
backstage: SYSREQ-012: initializePlatform() called at service startup registering Configuration Service, Event Service, and Value Service
SYSREQ-023: Structured JSON logging captures startup sequence including SDK initialization steps
steps.thinking: "I need to verify that initializePlatform() executed cleanly and that every expected ADSP service dependency is registered before I can sign off on platform compliance."
steps.emotionalContext: Methodical and focused; this is a checklist-driven gate with clear pass/fail criteria. Confidence is moderate until the log evidence confirms each registration.
painPoints: Startup log verbosity may require manual scanning to locate SDK initialization entries among general application logs
No structured compliance report output means registration completeness must be inferred from log patterns
opportunities: A dedicated /health/ready response payload exposing ADSP SDK registration status would reduce manual log scanning
A structured compliance manifest emitted at startup would accelerate platform onboarding reviews aligned with SYSREQ-008

steps.action: Verify RabbitMQ domain event registration by inspecting the ADSP Event Service configuration and confirming session-created, session-updated, and hypothesis-generated events are registered
needs: Access to ADSP Event Service registration records for planner-service
Expected event schema definitions for session-created, session-updated, and hypothesis-generated events
frontstage: Event Service registration listing for planner-service showing registered event types
ADSP platform Event Service administration interface
backstage: SYSREQ-011: planner-service publishes session-created, session-updated, and hypothesis-generated domain events
SYSREQ-008: Domain event registration is a mandatory ADSP platform service compliance requirement
steps.thinking: "I need to confirm all three domain events are registered with correct schemas — missing or mismatched event registration could cause downstream consumer failures across the platform."
steps.emotionalContext: Diligent and precise; event schema mismatches have platform-wide impact so each registration detail matters.
painPoints: Cross-referencing event registrations with expected schemas requires consulting both planner-service documentation and the ADSP Event Service administration interface separately
opportunities: Automated event schema validation against a service-owned schema manifest would eliminate manual cross-referencing and accelerate compliance verification

steps.action: Confirm Keycloak JWT authentication configuration by checking realm settings, RS256 algorithm enforcement, JWKS endpoint caching behavior, and that the three required RBAC roles are defined
needs: Access to Keycloak realm configuration for the planner-service client
SYSREQ-009 and SYSREQ-013 requirements for JWT validation and RBAC role definitions
steps.touchpoint: Keycloak JWT Authorization Server — INT-008 integration
frontstage: Keycloak realm administration console showing planner-service client configuration
Role definitions for planner-user, planner-admin, and tenant-admin
backstage: SYSREQ-009: passport-jwt validates RS256 JWT; JWKS endpoint cached; invalid tokens return HTTP 401
SYSREQ-013: Three-level RBAC — planner-user, planner-admin, tenant-admin; missing role returns HTTP 403
steps.thinking: "I need to verify that all three RBAC roles exist in the realm, RS256 is enforced, and the JWKS cache TTL is set appropriately to avoid stale key failures."
steps.emotionalContext: Careful and thorough; Keycloak misconfiguration is a security risk that can silently pass authentication while enabling unauthorized access.
painPoints: JWKS cache TTL verification requires inspecting service configuration values rather than a directly visible Keycloak setting
Role mapping must be manually verified across both Keycloak and the planner-service authorization middleware
opportunities: A planner-service configuration endpoint exposing JWT validation settings in non-secret form would reduce manual cross-referencing effort
RBAC role matrix documentation in the service README would speed this verification step aligned with SYSREQ-013

steps.action: Execute cross-tenant access test scenarios against the planner-service REST API to verify tenantId filter enforcement on all MongoDB queries and confirm HTTP 403 is returned on cross-tenant access attempts
needs: Test tenant credentials for two distinct tenants
Access to planner-service REST API (v1) in a test environment
SYSREQ-007 expected behavior specification: HTTP 403 on cross-tenant access
frontstage: API responses to cross-tenant session access attempts showing HTTP 403 status codes
Test harness output confirming tenant boundary enforcement across session, business model, and hypothesis endpoints
backstage: SYSREQ-007: tenantId filter applied on all MongoDB queries; cross-tenant access returns HTTP 403
SN-007: Multi-tenant data isolation enforced at API and database layers
steps.thinking: "A single bypass of tenant isolation would be a critical security incident — I need to test boundary conditions, not just happy-path scenarios."
steps.emotionalContext: High-stakes and vigilant; multi-tenant isolation failures are the most severe compliance gap in a shared-platform service. Rigorous testing here prevents platform-wide data exposure.
painPoints: No automated cross-tenant isolation test suite is included with the service — manual test case construction is required for each review cycle
Reproducing edge cases such as ObjectId overlap across tenants requires deep knowledge of the MongoDB document structure
opportunities: A platform-provided multi-tenant isolation test harness would standardize this verification across all ADSP services
Service-level integration tests targeting SYSREQ-007 scenarios could be run as part of the platform onboarding pipeline

steps.action: Review MongoDB query implementation to confirm tenantId is present in every database query filter and that no cross-tenant data leakage is possible through aggregation pipelines or index scans
needs: Access to planner-service source code repository
SYSREQ-007 compliance criteria for tenantId enforcement at the database layer
steps.touchpoint: planner-service source code repository and MongoDB Mongoose model definitions
frontstage: Source code review showing tenantId field presence in all Mongoose query filters
MongoDB collection index definitions confirming compound indexes include tenantId
backstage: SYSREQ-007: All MongoDB queries include tenantId filter enforced via Mongoose middleware or explicit filter injection
SN-007: Database-layer isolation must be independently verifiable from API-layer enforcement
steps.thinking: "API-layer enforcement alone is not sufficient — I need to see that even if the middleware were bypassed, the database queries themselves would not return cross-tenant data."
steps.emotionalContext: Analytical and methodical; code review requires concentration and pattern recognition across the entire data access layer.
painPoints: Large service codebases require systematic review tooling to confirm tenantId presence across all query sites — manual review is error-prone at scale
opportunities: A linting rule or static analysis check enforcing tenantId filter presence in all Mongoose queries would provide continuous compliance assurance between review cycles

steps.action: Configure RBAC role policies and session inactivity timeout settings via the ADSP Configuration Service for the planner-service deployment
needs: ADSP Configuration Service access with platform-admin or tenant-admin role
SYSREQ-013 RBAC role definitions and organizational session timeout policy values
steps.touchpoint: ADSP Configuration Service integration — planner-service configuration namespace
frontstage: Configuration Service interface showing planner-service configuration namespace
Role policy definitions and session inactivity timeout configuration values
backstage: SYSREQ-008: Configuration Service integration is a mandatory ADSP platform pattern
SYSREQ-013: RBAC role policies govern planner-user, planner-admin, and tenant-admin access levels
steps.thinking: "I need to set the session timeout to a value that balances security with usability for multi-day planning sessions — too short will frustrate users, too long is an ASVS violation."
steps.emotionalContext: Considered and deliberate; configuration decisions have long-term operational impact and require balancing security policy with user experience requirements.
painPoints: No documented recommended values for session inactivity timeout — must determine appropriate value from OWASP ASVS requirements and GoA security policy independently
opportunities: Platform-provided default configuration templates for common ADSP service security settings would reduce per-service configuration decision burden

steps.action: Record compliance verification findings and approve planner-service for production deployment by issuing formal platform sign-off
needs: Completed checklist of all ADSP platform pattern verifications
Documentation channel for recording compliance sign-off decision and evidence
steps.touchpoint: ADSP platform internal governance and deployment approval process
frontstage: Platform compliance checklist with all items verified and evidence recorded
Formal production deployment approval issued in the ADSP platform governance system
backstage: SYSREQ-008: Platform compliance verification is a mandatory gate before production deployment
SN-008: ADSP platform service compliance verification ensures consistent operational model across all platform services
steps.thinking: "All checks are complete and the service meets the platform requirements — I can issue the sign-off with confidence that planner-service will operate within the ADSP operational model."
steps.emotionalContext: Satisfied and confident; completing a thorough compliance review with positive findings is professionally rewarding and provides assurance to the wider platform.
painPoints: Compliance sign-off process is manual and lacks automated tracking — findings must be documented in a separate system outside the platform tooling
opportunities: An automated compliance dashboard tracking ADSP platform pattern verification status across all services would reduce manual documentation overhead
Integrating the compliance checklist into the ADSP service catalog would provide persistent audit evidence for each service version

journeys.outcome: planner-service receives ADSP platform compliance sign-off and is promoted to production operating within the standard platform operational model without special-casing

journeys.name: Ongoing Monitoring and Incident Response
journeys.description: The ADSP Platform Team routinely monitors planner-service health, structured observability endpoints, and LLM API performance metrics. When anomalies or degradation are detected, they investigate using structured logs and health endpoints and then coordinate remediation steps to restore service.
journeys.trigger: An automated platform monitoring alert fires indicating service degradation, or a scheduled routine health review window is reached
journeys.goal: Detect and resolve planner-service operational issues including LLM API degradation through structured observability data

steps.action: Check planner-service liveness and readiness endpoints to confirm the service is accepting traffic and all dependencies are reachable
needs: Access to planner-service health endpoints /health/live and /health/ready
Baseline readiness criteria including MongoDB, RabbitMQ, and Anthropic Claude API reachability checks
frontstage: /health/live response confirming the process is alive
/health/ready response showing dependency health status including MongoDB, RabbitMQ, and LLM API reachability
backstage: SYSREQ-023: Health check endpoints return structured JSON responses; /health/ready includes dependency connectivity checks
INT-001: Anthropic Claude API availability is a critical external dependency for all planning session functionality
steps.thinking: "If readiness is failing I need to know which dependency is the root cause — the health endpoint response must give me that granularity or I am starting blind on the incident."
steps.emotionalContext: Alert and focused; health check review is rapid triage and the speed of this step directly determines how quickly an incident is contained and resolved.
painPoints: If /health/ready returns unhealthy without per-dependency breakdown, root cause identification requires jumping directly to log analysis without a clear starting point
LLM API health is externally dependent on Anthropic service status and is outside the platform team's direct control or remediation
opportunities: Per-dependency health status in the /health/ready response body for MongoDB, RabbitMQ, and LLM API would reduce triage time from minutes to seconds
Integration with the ADSP platform monitoring dashboard to surface planner-service health alongside other platform services

steps.action: Review structured JSON logs to identify error patterns, elevated latency events, and LLM API performance degradation within the current monitoring window
needs: Access to planner-service structured JSON log stream via the ADSP platform log aggregation system
Log query capability to filter by error level, LLM API response times, and tenant context
SYSREQ-023 structured logging field schema for query construction
steps.touchpoint: planner-service structured JSON logging output via ADSP platform log aggregation
frontstage: Structured JSON log entries with severity, timestamp, tenant context, and operation identifiers
LLM API response time metrics logged per request for latency trend analysis
backstage: SYSREQ-023: All application log entries are structured JSON with a consistent field schema
INT-001: LLM API latency directly affects streaming response quality for all active planning conversations
steps.thinking: "I am looking for patterns — a single slow LLM response is noise, but a sustained increase in p95 latency is a signal that needs attention before users start reporting degraded experience."
steps.emotionalContext: Investigative and pattern-seeking; log analysis requires sustained concentration and the ability to distinguish noise from signal across high-volume log streams.
painPoints: Structured log query tools may not be purpose-built for LLM API latency percentile analysis without custom query construction
Correlating LLM API degradation with specific tenant activity requires joining log entries across multiple event types
opportunities: Pre-built log query templates for common planner-service operational scenarios such as LLM latency spikes and MongoDB error bursts would accelerate routine monitoring
A dedicated LLM API performance metrics endpoint would expose aggregated latency data without requiring log parsing on every review cycle

steps.action: Isolate the affected component — LLM API, MongoDB, RabbitMQ, or application code — by correlating health endpoint data with structured log error events to establish the incident root cause
needs: Health endpoint data from the current incident window
Structured log error events with component context and timestamp correlation
ADSP platform runbook for planner-service incident response
steps.touchpoint: planner-service Health Check Endpoints and structured JSON logging
frontstage: Correlated health and log data pinpointing the failing component
Timeline of error events relative to the incident onset for root cause determination
backstage: SYSREQ-023: Structured JSON logging provides traceable event sequences enabling incident correlation
INT-001: External Anthropic Claude API failures manifest as LLM_API_ERROR log entries with HTTP status codes
steps.thinking: "The degradation started at a specific timestamp — I need to see what changed in the logs at that exact moment to determine whether this is an LLM API outage or a service-side regression."
steps.emotionalContext: Urgent and pressured; active incident investigation requires quick decisions with incomplete information while minimizing service impact duration.
painPoints: External LLM API incidents require waiting for Anthropic service status updates — the platform team has no direct remediation lever beyond circuit-breaking or disabling the feature
Correlating multi-component failures without distributed tracing significantly increases mean time to isolation
opportunities: Adding distributed trace IDs to planner-service log entries would reduce incident isolation time and enable end-to-end request tracing
A graceful degradation mode for LLM API unavailability providing an informative error instead of silent failure would reduce user impact during external outages

steps.action: Execute the appropriate remediation action — restart the degraded pod, apply a configuration change, or coordinate with Anthropic support — and verify service restoration via health endpoints
needs: Kubernetes pod management access for planner-service workload
ADSP Configuration Service write access for configuration-driven remediations
Clear service restoration criteria for incident closure
steps.touchpoint: planner-service Health Check Endpoints and ADSP platform Kubernetes management interface
frontstage: Post-remediation /health/ready response confirming all dependencies are healthy
Structured log stream showing error rate return to baseline levels
backstage: SYSREQ-023: Health endpoints drive Kubernetes liveness and readiness probes for automated pod lifecycle management
SYSREQ-008: Service restarts must re-execute initializePlatform() to restore all ADSP SDK registrations
steps.thinking: "After the restart I need to confirm that initializePlatform() completed again — a partially initialized service can look healthy on the liveness probe while missing event registrations."
steps.emotionalContext: Cautiously optimistic; post-remediation verification is a critical step that prevents premature incident closure and recurrence.
painPoints: Post-restart initializePlatform() completion is not directly surfaced by the health endpoints — log review is required to confirm SDK re-registration after each restart
opportunities: Exposing ADSP SDK initialization status in the /health/ready response payload would make post-restart verification immediate and unambiguous, aligning SYSREQ-008 and SYSREQ-023

journeys.outcome: planner-service restored to healthy operational state with root cause documented, service impact period recorded, and structural improvements identified to prevent recurrence

journeys.name: Security Review and Audit Log Verification
journeys.description: The ADSP Platform Team conducts periodic security reviews of the planner-service covering HMAC-chained audit log integrity verification, OWASP ASVS Level 2 conformance assessment, and RBAC enforcement validation. Reviews support GoA compliance reporting and incident investigation readiness.
journeys.trigger: Scheduled periodic security review cycle or a compliance audit request from GoA security governance
journeys.goal: Validate OWASP ASVS Level 2 conformance, verify HMAC audit log chain integrity, and produce a security review report for compliance records

stages.name: Audit Log Access and Integrity Verification

steps.action: Access the planner-service audit log endpoint and retrieve the audit event records for the review period
needs: Platform-admin role granting access to the planner-service audit log API endpoint
Review period date range for audit log retrieval
SYSREQ-020 specification for audit log structure and HMAC chaining field definitions
steps.touchpoint: planner-service REST API (v1) — audit log endpoint
frontstage: Paginated audit event records with timestamp, actorId, tenantId, action, and HMAC chain fields
Audit log API response confirming successful record retrieval for the specified period
backstage: SYSREQ-020: HMAC-chained audit log records every security-relevant event; chain enables tamper detection
SN-012: Security audit logging is required for GoA compliance posture for Protected B information systems
steps.thinking: "I need the full record set for the review period — any gaps in the audit log sequence are themselves a finding that must be reported regardless of other review outcomes."
steps.emotionalContext: Precise and compliance-oriented; audit log access is the foundation of the security review and any retrieval failure is immediately material to the review outcome.
painPoints: Large audit log volumes for high-activity tenants require pagination handling that slows the retrieval step
No dedicated bulk audit log export format — retrieval requires API pagination rather than a single structured export operation
opportunities: A bulk audit log export endpoint accepting date range parameters would simplify retrieval for periodic security reviews
Integration with the ADSP platform centralized audit log aggregation service would eliminate per-service retrieval workflows

steps.action: Verify the HMAC chain integrity across the retrieved audit log records to confirm no records have been tampered with or deleted since original logging
needs: Retrieved audit event records with HMAC chain fields
HMAC verification tooling and shared secret access restricted to platform-admin
SYSREQ-020 HMAC chaining algorithm specification
steps.touchpoint: planner-service audit log records and HMAC verification tooling
frontstage: HMAC chain verification result indicating overall chain integrity status
Identification of any broken chain links indicating potential tampering events or missing records
backstage: SYSREQ-020: Each audit log entry includes an HMAC computed over the current record and previous record hash enabling sequential tamper detection
SN-012: Tamper-evident audit logging is a security compliance requirement for GoA Protected B information systems
steps.thinking: "A broken HMAC chain is a security incident indicator, not just a data quality issue — if I find a chain break I need to immediately assess whether it represents unauthorized deletion or system corruption."
steps.emotionalContext: Highly focused and alert; HMAC verification is a binary security signal and any chain failure requires immediate escalation to the security incident process.
painPoints: HMAC verification requires custom tooling or scripting — no platform-provided audit log integrity checker exists for SYSREQ-020 compliant services
Determining whether a chain break is operational such as a crash during write versus adversarial requires additional forensic investigation beyond the chain check itself
opportunities: A platform-provided HMAC chain verification utility for SYSREQ-020 compliant services would standardize integrity checking across all ADSP audit logs
Continuous background chain integrity monitoring would surface tampering in near-real-time rather than only at periodic review intervals

steps.action: Assess planner-service against OWASP ASVS Level 2 control requirements covering authentication, session management, access control, and API security clusters
needs: OWASP ASVS 4.0 Level 2 control checklist
SYSREQ-018 conformance requirements and evidence criteria
Access to planner-service configuration, API behavior documentation, and authentication flow specifications
steps.touchpoint: planner-service REST API (v1), Keycloak JWT Authorization Server (INT-008), and planner-service technical documentation
frontstage: ASVS Level 2 control checklist with planner-service assessment findings recorded per control
Evidence artifacts including API response headers, authentication flow logs, and configuration values
backstage: SYSREQ-018: OWASP ASVS Level 2 conformance is the mandatory security baseline for this Protected B GoA information system
SYSREQ-009: Keycloak JWT RS256 validation directly addresses ASVS authentication controls
SYSREQ-013: Three-level RBAC directly addresses ASVS access control controls
steps.thinking: "ASVS Level 2 has over a hundred controls — I need to prioritize the authentication, session management, and data protection clusters first since those are most likely to surface gaps in a new service."
steps.emotionalContext: Thorough and systematic; ASVS assessment is high-effort compliance work requiring sustained concentration with significant security implications if control gaps are missed.
painPoints: ASVS Level 2 assessment is a significant time investment with more than 100 controls and no automated assessment tooling maps directly to this service technology stack
Some ASVS controls require dynamic testing such as session fixation and token replay that must be conducted in a staging environment with controlled test data
opportunities: A planner-service ASVS control mapping document as a SYSREQ-018 evidence package would allow reviewers to focus on high-risk controls rather than rechecking established patterns
Automated security scanning integrated into the service CI/CD pipeline would provide continuous ASVS coverage for programmatically detectable vulnerabilities

steps.action: Verify RBAC enforcement is correctly applied across all API endpoints by testing role-permission boundaries for planner-user, planner-admin, and tenant-admin roles
needs: Test accounts provisioned for each of the three RBAC roles
SYSREQ-013 role permission matrix specifying allowed operations per role
planner-service REST API (v1) complete endpoint list
steps.touchpoint: planner-service REST API (v1) — protected endpoints with role-based access control
frontstage: API responses showing HTTP 403 for role-insufficient requests across all protected endpoints
Role permission boundary test results confirming planner-user, planner-admin, and tenant-admin access levels are correctly enforced
backstage: SYSREQ-013: Authorization middleware enforces role-based access at each endpoint; missing required role returns HTTP 403
SN-012: RBAC enforcement is a platform compliance requirement verified during all security reviews
steps.thinking: "I need to test the permission boundaries systematically — that planner-user cannot reach admin endpoints, that planner-admin cannot exceed tenant-admin capabilities, and that no role escalation path exists."
steps.emotionalContext: Precise and boundary-focused; RBAC testing requires methodical coverage of the full permission matrix to avoid gaps that could enable privilege escalation.
painPoints: Manual RBAC testing across all endpoints and three role levels requires constructing many individual test cases with no automated RBAC test suite provided with the service
opportunities: An RBAC test matrix document accompanying the service specifying expected HTTP response codes per endpoint per role would reduce manual test case construction effort
Automated RBAC boundary testing as part of the service integration test suite would provide ongoing assurance aligned with SYSREQ-013

steps.action: Document security review findings, record HMAC chain verification results, ASVS gap assessments, and RBAC test outcomes in the security review report
needs: Completed findings from all preceding assessment steps
Security review report template aligned with GoA security governance requirements
ADSP audit trail access for recording the security review event
steps.touchpoint: ADSP platform internal security review documentation system and planner-service audit log
frontstage: Security review report with findings organized by ASVS control cluster and severity rating
Audit log entry recording the security review event with reviewer identity and timestamp
backstage: SYSREQ-020: Administrative and security review actions are logged in the HMAC-chained audit log
SN-012: Security review completion must itself be auditable for GoA compliance reporting purposes
steps.thinking: "Every finding needs a severity rating and a remediation recommendation — partial findings with no actionable guidance are useless to the development team and do not satisfy compliance records."
steps.emotionalContext: Responsible and thorough; security report authoring carries professional accountability and must be defensible under external audit scrutiny.
painPoints: No standardized security review report template exists for ADSP services — each review requires independent format decisions that reduce cross-service comparability
Documenting ASVS gap findings requires accurately citing control numbers and severity without a pre-mapped evidence package from the service
opportunities: A standardized ADSP security review report template covering ASVS, HMAC audit, and RBAC sections would reduce documentation effort and improve findings comparability across services
Persisting the security review report in the ADSP service catalog alongside the compliance checklist would maintain a longitudinal compliance record per service

steps.action: Issue security review sign-off and communicate findings to the planner-service development team including any required remediation actions before the next review cycle
needs: Completed and approved security review report
Communication channel to the planner-service development team
Clear severity classification for any identified gaps requiring remediation
steps.touchpoint: ADSP platform governance communication channels and ADSP GitHub Issues repository
frontstage: Formal security review sign-off recorded in the ADSP governance system
Findings report delivered to the planner-service development team via GitHub Issues or direct channel
backstage: SN-012: Security review outcomes feed into the GoA compliance reporting cycle for Protected B information systems
SYSREQ-018: OWASP ASVS Level 2 gaps require tracked remediation before the next compliance cycle closes
steps.thinking: "If there are critical findings the development team needs them immediately with clear remediation guidance — a well-structured findings report reduces back-and-forth and accelerates resolution."
steps.emotionalContext: Professionally accountable and collaborative; the sign-off signals completion of the review obligation while the findings communication initiates the remediation partnership.
painPoints: No integrated findings tracking between the security review process and the development team backlog — gaps must be manually translated into GitHub Issues
Severity classification requires judgment calls that may differ between reviewers without a standardized ADSP severity rubric
opportunities: Automated creation of GitHub Issues from security review findings would close the loop between security review completion and development team remediation tracking
A shared ADSP security severity rubric would standardize finding classification across all platform service security reviews

journeys.outcome: Security review report produced with HMAC chain integrity confirmed, OWASP ASVS Level 2 conformance assessed, RBAC boundaries validated, and all findings communicated to the development team with severity ratings and remediation guidance
